What Job A fixed, and what it did not
PTX3 is transformed. rs2305619 went from 15 poolable rows and 2 with genotype counts to 45 and 32; rs3816527 from 20 and 8 to 39 and 31; rs1840680 from 6 and 1 to 36 and 30. Most of that comes from Tang 2020, whose full genotype tables sat beyond the old character cap.
TLR4 is not fixed and cannot be fixed by extraction. rs4986790 now has 9 studies and 2 poolable rows; rs4986791 has 9 studies and 1. Fisher 2017 analysed both but published no estimate or counts for either — they are in its supplemental Table 1, which is not in the supplied PDF. Fischer 2016 did not genotype them. Konuma 2026 notes both are close to monomorphic in Asian populations. The binding constraint is the missing supplementary files, not the extraction, so TLR4 needs supplementary retrieval or author contact before the haplotype block can be parameterised.
Four studies have supplementary tables that are absent from the supplied PDFs and hold genotype counts or null estimates: S049 (Suppl. Tables III and IV), S080 (supplemental Table 1), S027 (Table S1), S071 (Table S1).


Provisional rows
33 rows were transcribed by the extracting agents directly from the full text after their model-call budgets were exhausted, rather than produced by a model pass: S075’s 12 ARNT2/CX3CR1 haplotype rows read from Table 3, S073’s 7 reference-group rows whose counts are derived by subtraction from printed category totals, S034’s 6 TLR rows, S027’s 3 Table 6 haplotype rows plus the rs7525979 excluded-variant row, S057’s 2 genotyped-but-excluded rows, and S080’s 2 analysed-but-no-estimate rows. Each carries extraction_method = agent_read_not_model_extracted and a note naming it as such. All 33 are flagged P1 in the round-2 list and should be checked first.


Three variant-identification errors resolved from source
Round 1’s flagged “missing” rsIDs included several that are typographical errors in the papers themselves, now confirmed and captured under the correct identifier: rs7931529 is a Table 3 column-header typo in Lupiañez 2020 for rs7631529; rs6744330 is a Results-text typo in Gonçalves 2021 for rs674430; rs381627 is a table-footnote typo in Tang 2020 for rs3816527; rs47933 in Zhong 2022 is a truncation of NLRC4 rs479333. Separately, rs6535939 and rs61329579 are retired rs numbers for TLR2 rs4585282, stated as such in Skonieczna 2017’s own Discussion.
Cunha 2017’s 25 apparently-missed rsIDs were correctly not extracted: they appear only in the “SNPs tagged” and LD-proxy columns of its supplementary tables. The paper genotyped five variants and five were captured. Round 1 was right there.

The important finding is that the TLR4 problem was partly a question of looking for the wrong field. Three studies (Ceesay 2016, Kalkanci 2020, Grube 2013) print complete 2x3 genotype tables for both TLR4 SNPs and no odds ratio at all — they report only a chi-squared or Fisher p. Two more (Aki 2015, Tanpaibule 2020) add partial or complete counts. An odds ratio under any genetic model can be computed from those counts, so these are not author-contact targets.
The structural catch is that every one of these cohorts has zero minor homozygotes in both cases and controls for rs4986790 and rs4986791 — for example Grube 2013 rs4986790 is 0/6/35 in cases and 0/7/100 in controls. Only a dominant or carrier model is estimable, and a continuity correction will be needed. Two expectations were wrong and are corrected here.
Fisher 2017’s supplemental Table 1 is genotyping and imputation quality control, not effect estimates — alleles, minor allele frequency, call rate, Hardy-Weinberg p and pass/fail across three cohorts for 25 SNPs. It does not advance TLR4 on the estimate route. What it does deliver is 25 nucleotide allele pairs with per-cohort frequencies, which makes it the review’s single largest allele source, since many SNPs carry effect estimates elsewhere in the table with no alleles attached. Two cautions: the Alleles column carries no footnote defining major/minor order, and it disagrees with Schnetzke 2024’s explicitly major/minor listing for rs3816527 (C/A against A/C), so the order cannot be assumed. Five SNPs failed QC in Cohort 1 only — rs4833095, rs767455, rs3901533, rs4804800, rs7252229.
Schnetzke 2024’s Table S2 gives three-genotype distributions for the stratification (n=186) and validation (n=138) cohorts but does not split them by invasive fungal disease status, so no 2x2 can be reconstructed and the per-genotype case and control counts remain unavailable. genotype_counts_available is corrected to no for that study. rs1840680 does not appear in Table S2 at all, only in a footnote stating complete linkage disequilibrium with rs2305619.
Brunel 2018 delivered what was expected, and it bears directly on Aim 3b. Supplementary Figure 2 reports rs2305619 and rs3816527 separately, which the main paper did not, in three strata: all episodes, no neutropenia at presentation, and neutropenia at presentation. The non-neutropenic result that the combined hazard ratio of 5.06 came from decomposes into rs2305619 homozygous 8/33 versus other 7/100 (P=0.008) and rs3816527 homozygous 9/37 versus other 5/92 (P=0.002), against P=0.7 and P=0.6 in the neutropenic stratum. No per-SNP hazard ratio is printed anywhere — all three Cox models in Supplementary Table 1 use the combined “and/or” variable.
Herrero-Sanchez 2018 carries a scope caveat recorded on every row: none of its supplementary tables uses proven or probable invasive mould disease as the endpoint. 6. Baseline model — verified, with one gap
Everything needed is in the Stanzani paper and has been re-read from it: the equation and intercept, each predictor’s prevalence separately in cases and non-cases, and the validation targets.
The joint distribution of the seven predictors is not published, and it is load-bearing. Sampling 200,000 admissions independently from the published marginals and applying the fixed equation gives an IMD prevalence of 2.27% against 3.3%, and an aROC of 0.775 against 0.85. High-risk chemotherapy and prolonged neutropenia are close to the same clinical state and cannot be drawn independently.

rho = 0.30 reproduces both global targets almost exactly but misses the per-predictor case-group prevalences — uncontrolled malignancy 74% simulated against 59% published, corticosteroids 38% against 23%, high-risk chemotherapy 54% against 64%. One exchangeable parameter spreads correlation evenly across pairs that are clinically very differently related, so a structured matrix fitted to the 16 published targets is needed, with clinical constraints to make it identifiable.
Worth requesting from Bologna: 2x2 cross-tabulations for chemotherapy x neutropenia, neutropenia x lymphopenia and malignancy status x chemotherapy, plus the distribution of admissions per patient. That would convert an assumption into data.
Update, 17 October 2026 — correlation structure fitted. A structured latent correlation matrix (non-negative dependence, clinically grouped) was fitted to the 16 published targets. The first version had eight parameters and reduced chi-square against the targets from 346 under independence and 47 under the exchangeable rho = 0.30 to 8.6. Two problems remained: uncontrolled malignancy in cases was simulated at 69% against 59% published (2.3 standard errors), and two parameters sat at their upper bound because the chemotherapy-lymphopenia correlation was tied to the block baseline, which also set malignancy’s links. Version 2 adds a separate chemotherapy-lymphopenia parameter (nine in all) and lets the block extras reach 0.7. Chi-square falls to 0.36, the largest miss is 0.4 standard errors, and the malignancy residual is gone. The fitted matrix has malignancy almost uncorrelated with the rest of the block (about 0.04) and chemotherapy, neutropenia and lymphopenia at 0.69 to 0.74 with each other. d_chemo_neut sits at its 0.7 cap, but the loss is lowest there, so the cap is not costing fit. Positive definiteness is no longer limiting (smallest eigenvalue 0.26).
Read the near-zero chi-square with care. The 16 targets collapse to about nine independent constraints, since the non-case prevalences follow from the case prevalences and the overall prevalence, and the model now has nine parameters. A saturated fit is expected to be this good and does not validate the structure. A 150-matrix ensemble (six chains, R-hat at most 1.09) shows the parameters are wide: the chemotherapy-neutropenia extra 0.24 to 0.68, steroids-CMV 0.02 to 0.60, the malignancy-chemotherapy extra 0.01 to 0.42 (5th to 95th percentiles). The Bologna cross-tabulations, especially malignancy by chemotherapy, would turn these into data.
Decision curves for thresholds of 1 to 30% are now exact functions of the profile distribution, which comes from numerical integration of the fitted copula (no patient-level sampling). On the fitted cohort the minimum clinically important difference is +0.00428 net benefit at the 5% threshold (ensemble 90% range 0.00397 to 0.00460) and +0.00140 at 20% (0.00117 to 0.00167). Baseline net benefit at 5% is 0.01478, with 21.4 true and 125.7 false positives per 1,000 admissions and 14.7% flagged. The curves are step functions because there are only 128 clinical profiles. See scripts/01_fit_correlation.R, 02_correlation_ensemble.R and 03_decision_curves.R, and the baseline and decision-curve pages of the report website. The first-version outputs are kept in output/v1/.
Update, 18 October 2026 — baseline cohort switched to the empirical joint (D8). The admission-level derivation data (bs.xlsx, 4,127 admissions) reproduces Table 2 apart from two non-case counts that are one lower than published, and a refit recovers the published coefficients. Its real joint distribution shows the fitted copula is 0.098 away in total variation distance, with several correlations wrong in sign, so the copula is now a sensitivity analysis and the baseline cohort is the observed distribution of the 128 profiles (75 observed). The MCID rule is unchanged; its values on the empirical cohort are +0.00445 at 5% (bootstrap 90% 0.00412 to 0.00478) and +0.00142 at 20%, replacing +0.00428 and +0.00140. Admissions per patient and the rule defining the 4,127 admissions are still needed from Bologna. A full BOSCORE export with identifiers (8,660 rows) cannot be linked to the 4,127 admissions; a pseudonymised extract of it is in data/restricted/ (gitignored). See phase3_decisions.md addendum 2 and status.md.
Update, 18 October 2026 — base dataset reconciled and baseline cohort corrected (D9). boscore.xlsx, the parent of bs.xlsx, reconciles exactly: the seven predictors are the BOSCORE_* columns, the 4,127 are the rows complete on them, and id is the key. 49 admission numbers appear on two rows (an event row and a non-event twin with the same patient and profile), so the 4,127 rows are 4,078 unique admissions, and 133 of 4,078 is the paper’s 3.3%. The baseline cohort is now the 4,078 admissions in 1,945 patients, with patients resampled in the bootstrap. The MCID is +0.00404 at 5% (patient bootstrap 90% 0.00370 to 0.00438) and +0.00113 at 20%, against +0.00445 and +0.00142 on the 4,127 rows; results will be reported against both. Admissions per patient: 2.10 on average, 1,000 patients with one admission. The 49 twin pairs are confirmed as an artefact (addendum 5) and no request to Bologna remains open. See phase3_decisions.md addenda 3 to 5 and status.md.
Update, 18 October 2026 — outcome-risk sensitivity (addendum 4). Scoring the published equation’s decisions against a refit truth, a refit rule and the observed outcomes gives a primary MCID of +0.00452, +0.00458 and +0.00441, against the adopted +0.00404, and a secondary MCID of +0.00137, +0.00160 and +0.00142 against +0.00113. The adopted value is the lowest of the four, the intervals overlap, and the published coefficients lie inside the refit’s intervals. No decision changed; results will be reported against the 4,127-row MCID as well, which brackets these. See phase3_decisions.md addendum 4.
Update, 18 October 2026 — the baseline model is refit on the base cohort (D10). The clinical block is now a maximum-likelihood refit of the seven predictors on the 4,078 unique admissions (patient-clustered SE, patient bootstrap), replacing the published equation, which becomes a sensitivity analysis. aROC is 0.858 apparent and 0.853 optimism-corrected, the calibration slope is 0.97, and every published coefficient lies inside the refit’s 90% interval. The MCID is +0.00458 at 5% (bootstrap 90% 0.00387 to 0.00566) and +0.00160 at 20%, against +0.00404 and +0.00113 under the published equation. Aim 2 becomes estimating the baseline and comparing it with the published equation. See phase3_decisions.md addendum 6 and status.md.
Update, 18 October 2026 — PTX3 defined and the evidence mapping started (D11, addendum 7). h2 is the PTX3 chromosome class carrying A at rs2305619 (A-C-A, A-A-A, A-A-G; 48.2% in gnomAD NFE); h1 is G-A-G; rs1840680 A is the same class and rs3816527 C marks only A-C-A. Each study’s contrast is converted to a per-copy h2 effect by solving a haplotype model, one effect is taken per study, and the effects are pooled with a Bayesian random-effects model. Provisional PTX3 result from five studies: OR 1.35 per h2 copy (90% interval 0.99 to 1.81), tau 0.17. The rows are unverified and most mapping rules and the priors are proposals open to change. See phase3_decisions.md addendum 7 and status.md.
Update, 18 October 2026 — rows checked against sources, and the mapping extended to CLEC7A and TLR4 (addendum 8). Herrero-Sanchez 2018, read in full, has its reference label reversed in every table; the extraction followed it, so the study looked as if it pointed the other way, which was an artefact (30 rows corrected, and the addendum 7 statement retracted). Brunel 2018’s design is confirmed but its per-SNP counts cannot be checked from the text and may be the wrong homozygote group. Provisional primary results, as odds ratios per copy of the risk haplotype: PTX3 h2 1.35 (0.99 to 1.81), CLEC7A Y238X 0.98 (0.56 to 1.72), TLR4 G-T 1.44 (0.77 to 2.69). The second CLEC7A effect needs the strand of rs7309123 resolved for each study. See phase3_decisions.md addendum 8 and status.md.

6b. Phase 3 gate — settled 16 October 2026
Recipient genotype is the primary exposure, with donor genotype as a pre-specified secondary restricted to the allogeneic HSCT stratum. The panel is four haplotype terms — PTX3 (rs2305619/rs3816527/rs1840680), CLEC7A (rs16910526/rs7309123, 3 haplotypes), TLR4 (rs4986790/rs4986791) and CD209 (rs4804800/rs7248637, 4 haplotypes) — with IL10 rs1800896 and IFNG rs2069705 optional (both dropped on 19 October 2026, D14). The minimum clinically important difference is 20% more true cases of invasive mould disease at no increase in false positives. It was stated as +0.00420 net benefit at the 5% threshold and +0.00191 at 20% on an indicative cohort, and was re-derived on the calibrated cohort on 17 October 2026 as +0.00428 at 5% (primary) and +0.00140 at 20% (secondary). Full record in phase3_decisions.md. All sub-decisions are now settled (17 October 2026): 5% is the primary MCID threshold; TLR9 rs352140 is dropped (D3a); Herrero-Sanchez 2018 is excluded from the primary analysis and run as a sensitivity analysis (D3b); TLR4 is pooled under a carrier model with a continuity correction (D3c); the genetic term is recentred to hold prevalence (D5); the baseline aROC target is 0.85 (D6); and the haplotype phase is coupling, confirmed arithmetically (E1).
The CLEC7A and CD209 terms were collapsed from single SNPs to haplotypes after a linkage check: rs16910526 x rs7309123 sit at D’ = 1.000 with the Y238X allele entirely on one rs7309123 background, and rs4804800 x rs7248637 at r2 = 0.413, D’ = 0.671 with all four haplotypes present. Entering either pair as independent additive terms would repeat the predecessor thesis’s error within a different gene.

section: 6c. The genetic layer, Aims 3b and 4 (18 to 19 October 2026)
text:
6c. The genetic layer, Aims 3b and 4 (18 to 19 October 2026)
Everything below is provisional: the effects come from the provisional evidence mapping, and the design choices are proposals recorded in addenda 9 to 17 of phase3_decisions.md. Numbers are after the correction of Fischer 2016 (below).
Evidence mapping (addenda 7 to 9, 16). Pooled odds ratios per copy of each term’s risk haplotype class (primary analysis, 90% interval): PTX3 h2 1.35 (0.99 to 1.81, 5 studies), CLEC7A Y238X 0.84 (0.48 to 1.48, 4), TLR4 G-T 1.44 (0.77 to 2.69, 4), CD209 G at rs4804800 1.80 (1.14 to 2.73, 3). IL10 (one study) and IFNG (two, disagreeing) were dropped from the panel. The second CLEC7A parameter, the A-G haplotype (the G allele of rs7309123 on the non-Y238X background), is estimated at OR 1.8 per copy (1.07 to 2.71) from two strand-resolved European studies, and stays between 1.5 and 1.9 under every alternative strand assumption. The strand of rs7309123 in each of ten studies was determined from control frequencies and the papers (data/rs7309123_strand_resolution.csv): resolved with medium to high confidence for three, low to medium for one, weakly for three, undetermined for three (Kalkanci 2020, Chen 2019, Zhao 2022).
An error found and corrected (19 October, addendum 16 section 0). Fischer 2016 lists the reference group first in its table; the pipeline read the first group as the numerator, so its Y238X and rs7309123 effects were reversed. 12 rows are corrected with their evidence, the Y238X pooled OR moved from 0.98 to 0.84, and every script using CLEC7A was rerun: the layer gains moved by at most 0.00006. 139 rows in the four terms’ analyses were read from comparison text with no reference marker; the five used in primary analyses were inspected and the studies behind them have since been checked against their tables. The direction check (addendum 18) found Tang 2020 and Tanpaibule 2020 correct, one reversed row in Sainz 2012 (corrected), and could not confirm Chen 2019 or Fisher 2017 from the open text. Two earlier errors of the same family: Herrero-Sanchez 2018’s reversed reference label (addendum 8) and a first interaction model for Aim 3b that left out the neutropenia main effect (found and fixed during the run).
The genetic layer (addenda 11 to 14). On the base cohort with the refit baseline, genotype fixed per patient, each term’s risk-class dosage Hardy-Weinberg in gnomAD NFE frequencies, the true logit recentred to hold prevalence, the gain over the baseline computed exactly over 128 clinical profiles by the dosage combinations, for 2,000 draws of the true effects from the pooled posteriors: - Primary result. With the true effects in the score (the ceiling) the median gain is +0.0006 at 5% and +0.0010 at 20%; with the pooled estimates in the score (realised), +0.0004 and +0.0008. The MCID is +0.00458 at 5% (reached in at most about 1% of draws) and +0.00160 at 20% (reached in 16% of draws for the ceiling score, 3% for the realised score). - Sampling variability of a study of this size (4,078 admissions, 133 events): the standard deviation of the observed gain is 0.0006 to 0.0013 at 5%, as large as the expected gain or larger; an observed study reaches the 5% MCID in at most 5% of repetitions in any run. - Robustness. The 150-member correlation ensemble moves the gain by at most 0.00015 (between-member SD 0.0001 to 0.0003); the sensitivity cohorts (published equation on 4,078 or 4,127 rows, refit on 4,127 rows) change the gain little and change which MCID is reached at 20% (the published equation sets a lower bar). - Attribution (Shapley), four terms: CD209 supplies about 52% of the gain, PTX3 23%, TLR4 19%, CLEC7A 7%. - Donor genotype in the allo-HSCT stratum (D1 secondary, addenda 13 and 14). The base cohort now carries an admission-level allo flag (derived from the composite item SCORE9 and a transplant date; 292 admissions as in Table 1, 43 events against 44; 272 admissions and 43 events in the base cohort). Allo admissions are the high-risk chemotherapy item and only 23 of 128 profiles occur, so the baseline is nearly calibrated there (odds multiplier 1.15) and flags 77% of them at 5%. Donor genotype adds 0.4 to 1.4 true cases per 1,000 allo admissions at 5% against 30 needed, and 14 to 28 at 20% against about 11; the donor evidence is one study each for PTX3 and CLEC7A, two for TLR4, none for CD209. A smoothed stratum gives the same conclusions.
With the second CLEC7A parameter (addenda 16 and 17). CLEC7A becomes an active term. The gain roughly doubles (ceiling +0.0012 at 5%, +0.0017 at 20%, and the 20% MCID is reached in 57% of draws), and CLEC7A supplies about 48% of the Shapley gain, almost all through the A-G haplotype, with CD209 falling to 28%, PTX3 to 13% and TLR4 to 10%. This rests on two studies and is the least mature part of the evidence.
CLEC7A’s lead holds (addendum 18). The five-term attribution and Aim 3b layer, rerun on the three sensitivity cohorts and on the 150-member correlation ensemble, give CLEC7A about 48% of the gain in every setting (42.5% to 49.1% over every reading and threshold) and CD209 26% to 36%; CLEC7A is the largest single contributor in about half to 63% of draws. The neutropenic stratum supplies 78% to 83% of the gain at 5% and 95% to 97% at 20% in every setting.
Aim 3b, the neutropenia-stratified falsification test (addendum 15; five-term version in addendum 17). The expected direction was committed before the run. The Feys reading (effects larger in neutropenic admissions) and Brunel 2018’s stratified data (larger in non-neutropenic, difference P = 0.07 and 0.049) point opposite ways. Neutropenic admissions hold 80% of the events and supply 81% to 96% of the whole-cohort gain under homogeneous effects. A single score with the pooled estimates is the safe choice; a score built on the Feys reading is the most harmful when wrong. In simulated studies of the cohort’s size an interaction test is better powered than predicted (59% to 88% for a Feys-sized modification, 95% to 100% for Brunel-sized ones, false positives 5%). Of the five predictions, two held, one mostly held, one did not hold in general and one (that the test would be underpowered) was wrong.
Aim 4, the genetic-architecture requirements sweep (addenda 16 and 17). 1 to 20 identical independent loci x OR 1.1 to 3.0 x frequency 0.05 to 0.50, by exact convolution: 46% of the 4,000 architectures reach the 5% MCID and 77% the 20% MCID. At OR 1.5 or below no number of loci up to 20 reaches the 5% MCID; at OR 2.0 it takes 7 to 9 loci at common frequencies. The four-term panel is equivalent to about 7 loci of OR 1.3. With estimated weights (independent per-locus error, SD 0.05 to 0.40) precision of 0.1 or better costs almost nothing (a discovery sample of about 1,000 balanced subjects), while at 0.2 to 0.4, the precision of the present evidence, 12% to a third of the architectures that reach the MCID with exact weights no longer do.
Where the work lives. Scripts 01 to 25 in scripts/ (run order in status.md), the model code in R/, the test suite in tests/testthat/, results in output/, pinned packages in renv.lock. The repository is lewis-id-lab/PROSE (public); the Quarto site in docs/ is published to GitHub Pages on every push to main. No patient-level data are in the repository; the identified files were read locally with the user’s permission and only counts or a binary flag were kept (the pseudonymised base cohort is gitignored).

7. What is open

Round-2 verification. Add the record of the human checks to data/; obtain the full tables of Chen 2019 and Fisher 2017 to settle the direction of their text-parsed rows (the other studies are checked, addendum 18); decide the three questions left in addendum 8 (Herrero-Sanchez Table 5, Brunel’s counts and homozygote group, hazard-ratio studies).
rs7309123 strand. Three studies are undetermined (Kalkanci 2020, Chen 2019, Zhao 2022); two need their full texts or the authors. East Asian haplotype frequencies would let the Thai and Chinese studies enter the second parameter.
Cohort overlap. The Spanish registry series (Sainz / Lupiañez / Sánchez-Maldonado) and the Jena AML cohorts (S018, S023, S073; S023 is treated as the same cohort as S073) are not independent studies and have only been partly adjudicated.
Thin evidence. One to five studies per term; donor genotype one to two studies per term and none for CD209; TLR4’s supplementary retrieval (Fisher 2017’s supplement) is still outstanding; the priors on the pooled effect and on tau are proposals.
Choices to confirm. The reading of the “realised” score (addendum 11), the independence of genotype from the clinical profile, and the rule that the Brunel pattern applies to every term in Aim 3b.
Not done. The interaction test of Aim 3b on the sensitivity cohorts and the ensemble; the pathogen-specificity scenario of Aim 4; locus-specific error, winner’s curse and linkage in the sweep; a genotyped neutropenia-stratified analysis (the real test of Aim 3b); write-up.

8. Suggested order of work

Add the round-2 verification record to the repository and obtain the full tables of Chen 2019 and Fisher 2017 to close the direction check.
Resolve what can be resolved of the three undetermined strands, and decide whether to obtain East Asian haplotype frequencies.
Repeat Aim 3b and the attribution with five terms on the correlation ensemble and the sensitivity cohorts Done (addendum 18): CLEC7A’s lead and the neutropenia pattern hold.
Decide the write-up structure from the results above (the headline is that a four-term panel falls well short of the 5% MCID, and what architecture would not), with the figures of addenda 16 and 17.
Plan the genotyped, neutropenia-stratified study that the Aim 3b design analysis shows is feasible at this cohort size.

title: Evidence mapping
text:
What “h2” means
PTX3 has three loci in strong linkage (rs2305619, rs3816527, rs1840680). In the phased 1000 Genomes European data the common haplotypes are G-A-G (54%), A-C-A (40%) and A-A-A (6%), with alleles in that locus order.

h2 is the chromosome class that carries the A allele at rs2305619: A-C-A, A-A-A and the very rare A-A-G, 45.6% in 1000G EUR and 48.2% in gnomAD NFE. h1 is G-A-G. The model term is an additive per-copy effect of h2 in the recipient.
rs1840680 A is the same class (r² = 0.996), so it is an interchangeable tag.
rs3816527 C is not interchangeable. It marks only A-C-A, about 87% of h2, so evidence reported on it is mapped to h2 through the haplotype structure and used as a cross-check.

title: Evidence mapping
text:
How each study is converted
Studies report PTX3 in different ways: dominant or recessive contrasts, allelic odds ratios, or genotype counts, with the contrast sometimes written in both directions. Each one is converted to a single scale, the log odds ratio per h2 copy, by finding the effect that a haplotype model would need to produce the study’s contrast. The model is additive on the log-odds scale, uses Hardy-Weinberg haplotype pairs and case-control sampling, and the standard error follows by the delta method. The direction of each contrast is read from the comparison text, including which side is the reference.

title: Evidence mapping
text:
Limits

The rows are unverified except where stated above, and the checks so far are the assistant’s, not the human round-2 check.
Brunel 2018 states “the minor allele”, so its effect allele is inferred from European frequencies, and the frequency check above casts doubt on it.
The Chinese and Thai cohorts use European haplotype frequencies.
Three to five studies per term is few. The priors on the pooled effect and on tau are proposals.
Open questions from addendum 8 that the human checks did not settle: whether to use Herrero-Sanchez’s invasive aspergillosis rows and whether to keep Brunel in the primary analysis. The rs7309123 strand is resolved with some confidence for four of the ten studies and weakly for three more (addendum 16). Hazard-ratio studies join a term’s primary analysis only when it has fewer than three odds-ratio studies (addendum 9).

title: Baseline model reproduction
text:
What has to be reproduced
A synthetic cohort must reproduce 16 published targets: the IMD prevalence, the aROC, and the prevalence of each predictor separately in cases and non-cases. The paper does not publish the joint distribution of the seven predictors, and it is load-bearing. High-risk chemotherapy and prolonged neutropenia, for example, are close to the same clinical state and cannot be drawn independently.
I model the joint with a Gaussian copula: each predictor is a thresholded latent normal variable that keeps its published marginal prevalence, and the correlation of the latent variables is the assumption to be calibrated. Because the predictors are binary, every quantity of interest is a function of the 128 predictor profiles. The profile probabilities are computed by numerical integration of the 7-dimensional normal, so no patient-level sampling enters the results below.

title: Baseline model reproduction
text:
The fitted correlation structure
The matrix is structured by clinical grouping, with non-negative dependence. The marrow-suppression block (malignancy, chemotherapy, lymphopenia, neutropenia) shares a baseline correlation, with extra correlation allowed for the pairs that the requested Bologna cross-tabulations would cover. Steroids, CMV and prior mould disease are tied to the block by single parameters.

Version 1 and what went wrong with it
Version 1 had eight parameters. It left uncontrolled malignancy in cases simulated at 69% against 59% published (2.3 standard errors), and two block parameters sat at their upper bound. Both problems had one cause. Neutropenia is tightly tied to both chemotherapy and lymphopenia, which forces chemotherapy and lymphopenia to be correlated for the matrix to stay positive definite. In version 1 that pair shared the block baseline with malignancy’s links, so raising the baseline to satisfy the first pulled malignancy up with it.
Version 2 gives chemotherapy-lymphopenia its own parameter and lets the three block extras reach 0.7.

section: How well is the matrix identified?
text:
How well is the matrix identified?
Many matrices fit the targets about equally well. A random-walk Metropolis sampler on \(\exp(-\chi^2/2)\) gives an ensemble of near-optimal matrices (six chains, 400 retained draws each after thinning). It is not a formal posterior: the chi-square uses published sampling errors and ignores admission clustering.


Code
raw <- read.csv("output/correlation_ensemble_raw.csv")
rhat <- function(x, chain) {
  s <- split(x, chain); n <- length(s[[1]])
  W <- mean(sapply(s, var)); B <- n * var(sapply(s, mean))
  sqrt(((n - 1) / n * W + B / n) / W)
}
summ <- tibble(
  parameter = THETA_NAMES,
  q05 = sapply(THETA_NAMES, \(p) quantile(raw[[p]], 0.05)),
  median = sapply(THETA_NAMES, \(p) median(raw[[p]])),
  q95 = sapply(THETA_NAMES, \(p) quantile(raw[[p]], 0.95)),
  rhat = sapply(THETA_NAMES, \(p) rhat(raw[[p]], raw$chain))
)
ggplot(summ, aes(median, factor(parameter, rev(THETA_NAMES)))) +
  geom_pointrange(aes(xmin = q05, xmax = q95)) +

title: Baseline model reproduction
text:
Limitations

The correlation structure is an assumption fitted to published margins. It is not data. The real data now exist, and the copula is kept only as a sensitivity analysis.
The fit is saturated, so its quality said little about whether the structure was correct, and the comparison with the real data confirms it was not entirely.
The fitting loss uses binomial standard errors and ignores that the 4,127 admissions come from 1,944 patients.
The published aROC of 0.85 is apparent performance. The bootstrap-validated value is 0.83, and the MCID scales with baseline net benefit.
The distribution of admissions per patient is unpublished. It will be simulated and varied.
No genetic term has been added.

title: Genetic augmentation of a clinical risk model for invasive mould disease
text:
A validated clinical score (Stanzani et al., J Infect 2019) already predicts 60-day invasive mould disease (IMD) in haematological inpatients with an aROC of 0.85. Candidate host variants in PTX3, CLEC7A (dectin-1), CD209 (DC-SIGN), TLR4 and other genes are repeatedly reported as associated with invasive aspergillosis. This project asks whether adding them to the score would change what a clinician does.
It is framed as a value-of-information question rather than a prediction-improvement exercise:

Under what combinations of effect size, risk-allele frequency and linkage structure would host genetic information change clinical decisions for invasive mould disease in haematological patients, and is the published evidence anywhere near those combinations?

A negative answer, that no realistic genetic architecture moves the decision curve, is a finding and not a failure. The primary endpoint is decision-curve net benefit at the 5% threshold, judged against a minimum clinically important difference fixed before any genetic result exists.

Haplotype phase check
Haplotype frequencies were derived from allele frequencies and D, assuming the minor alleles are in coupling (D positive). D′ near 1 fixes the size of D but not its sign. The reported r² and the allele frequencies fix |D| independently of that assumption, so the sign can be checked arithmetically: if even the largest possible negative D is smaller than the |D| that r² requires, negative phase is impossible.

  group_by(gene, locus_1, locus_2) |>
  summarise(
    r2 = first(r2),
    p1 = sum(haplotype_freq_1000G_EUR[!allele_1 %in% c("major", "other")]),
    p2 = sum(haplotype_freq_1000G_EUR[!allele_2 %in% c("major", "other")]),
    .groups = "drop"

    required_D = sqrt(r2 * p1 * (1 - p1) * p2 * (1 - p2)),
    ceiling_if_negative = pmin(p1 * p2, (1 - p1) * (1 - p2)),
    negative_possible = required_D <= ceiling_if_negative + 1e-3

title: Decision curves and the MCID
text:
What “exact” means here
Net benefit at threshold \(t\) is the true-positive rate minus the false-positive rate weighted by \(t/(1-t)\). The baseline model has seven binary predictors, so there are only 128 predictor profiles, each with a known risk. Given the probability of each profile, net benefit at every threshold is an exact calculation: sort the profiles by risk, flag those at or above \(t\), and add up. No patient-level sample is drawn.
The profile probabilities come from numerical integration of the fitted 7-dimensional normal, not from simulating patients. The integrator (mvtnorm) uses a randomised quasi-Monte Carlo rule internally, with the error target set to \(10^{-7}\) per profile. Repeat runs with different seeds agree to about \(10^{-6}\), which is below any difference that matters here, and the test suite checks this.
The same code takes separate “decision” and “outcome” risks, so once genetic terms enter the data-generating model it can score a clinical-only rule against the true risk without change.






ImportantThe curve and bands below come from the fitted copula



Since decisions D9 and D10 (18 October 2026), the baseline cohort for the genetic layer is the observed distribution of the clinical profiles in the 4,078 unique admissions of boscore.xlsx (the 49 non-event twin rows removed), with patients resampled in the bootstrap, and the baseline model is a refit on that cohort. The curve and bands below are the copula’s with the published equation, a sensitivity analysis. The MCID table at the end of this page shows the adopted refit values next to the earlier ones.

Results are for the baseline alone. No genetic term has been added.

section: D1. Primary genotype — settled: recipient primary, donor secondary in the allo-HSCT stratum
text:
D1. Primary genotype — settled: recipient primary, donor secondary in the allo-HSCT stratum
Agreed 16 October 2026. Recipient genotype is the primary exposure. Donor genotype enters as a pre-specified secondary analysis restricted to the allogeneic HSCT stratum, which carries 33% of all IMD events on 7% of admissions, and which gives Aim 3b a second host-context contrast alongside the neutropenia split. The reasoning that forced the revision is kept below for the record.
Originally stated: donor genotype as the primary exposure.
The biology supports you, the cohort does not. After allogeneic transplant the reconstituted innate immune system is donor-derived, so for PTX3, dectin-1 and the TLR genes the donor is arguably the right genome — that is the Cunha 2014 NEJM argument. But two facts block donor as the primary exposure:

The baseline cohort is overwhelmingly not transplanted. In Stanzani’s Table 1, allogeneic HSCT is the reason for admission in 248 of 3,994 non-IMD admissions and 44 of 133 IMD admissions — 292 of 4,127 admissions, 7.1%. Donor genotype is undefined for the other 93%. A donor-genotype term cannot enter a model whose denominator is all haematology admissions.
The evidence base cannot parameterise it. Of 970 usable variant rows, only 90 are donor-stratified. Per panel variant, the number of studies contributing a donor-specific usable estimate is at most one, and rs4804800 and rs1840680 have none. No panel variant reaches two donor studies, let alone three.

Donor-as-primary would therefore shrink the analysis to a 7% subgroup — 292 admissions, 44 events — parameterised from single studies.
Proposed instead: recipient genotype as the primary exposure, with donor genotype as a pre-specified secondary analysis restricted to the allogeneic HSCT stratum. That stratum carries 33% of all IMD events despite being 7% of admissions, so it is where a genetic effect has the most room to show, and it is where the donor-genome argument actually applies. This also gives Aim 3b a second natural contrast alongside the neutropenia split.
☑ Revision confirmed.

section: D2. PTX3 and TLR4 as haplotypes — accepted
text:
D2. PTX3 and TLR4 as haplotypes — accepted
Consistent with the evidence and with the thesis’s central methodological correction.

PTX3 enters as a single h1/h2 haplotype term, not three SNPs. In 1000 Genomes EUR, rs2305619 and rs1840680 sit at r² = 0.996 and are interchangeable; rs3816527 is at r² ≈ 0.79 with both; D′ ≈ 1 throughout. The trio collapses to two haplotypes at roughly 0.40–0.46 (h2) and 0.54 (h1). Simulating the three independently is what inflated the predecessor’s result.
TLR4 enters as a single rs4986790–rs4986791 haplotype term. D′ = 0.981, r² = 0.945, GT haplotype frequency 0.056 in EUR, with about 0.3% recombinant chromosomes.

Parameter cost: these two blocks contribute 2 terms rather than 5.
☑ E1. Settled 16 October 2026 (arithmetic check): coupling confirmed. haplotype_frequencies.csv assumes the minor alleles are in coupling (D > 0). The reported r² and the allele frequencies fix |D| independently of that assumption, and for every pair |D| exceeds the largest value a negative D could take given those frequencies. For example, for rs2305619 x rs3816527 the r² of 0.787 requires |D| = 0.216, but a negative D cannot exceed 0.181. TLR4 (rs4986790 x rs4986791) needs 0.0524 against a negative-phase ceiling of 0.0033. CLEC7A and CD209 are likewise consistent only with D > 0. The check assumes r² and D′ were taken from the 1000G source and not back-calculated from the assumed D. Phased 1000G haplotypes remain the route for the three-locus PTX3 frequencies, but the sign is no longer an open question.

D5. How the genetic term enters the baseline model — settled: recentred
Settled 16 October 2026. The genetic linear predictor is recentred (equivalently, the intercept is adjusted) so that marginal IMD prevalence stays at the calibrated baseline value of 3.3%. Any change in net benefit therefore reflects discrimination and risk redistribution, not a shift in overall event rate.

Addendum, 17 October 2026
Written after the prespec-lock tag. No decision above is changed.
Haplotype frequencies were derived directly from phased 1000 Genomes phase 3 European genotypes (503 samples, 1,006 chromosomes; data/haplotype_frequencies_phased.csv) and rescaled to gnomAD v4 non-Finnish-European allele frequencies by iterative proportional fitting, which keeps the odds-ratio structure of the observed table and moves only the allele frequencies.

E1 is confirmed directly from phased chromosomes. In every pair the minor alleles are in coupling (D > 0), as the arithmetic check showed.
The earlier pairwise table is reproduced. Haplotype frequencies agree to within 0.0014, and r² agrees for PTX3, TLR4 and CLEC7A. For CD209, r² is 0.431 from phased data against 0.414 in the earlier table.
The PTX3 trio has three common haplotypes, not two. In 1000G EUR: G-A-G 54.4%, A-C-A 39.8%, A-A-A 5.8%, and a single A-A-G chromosome (alleles in the order rs2305619, rs3816527, rs1840680). Rescaled to gnomAD NFE: 51.8%, 42.4%, 5.6% and 0.1%. rs2305619 A and rs1840680 A mark the same haplotype class (r² = 0.996), which is A-C-A plus A-A-A (45.6% in 1000G, 48.2% in gnomAD NFE). rs3816527 C splits that class, and A-C-A is about 87% of it.

D2 stands as settled: PTX3 enters as a single h1/h2 term. The evidence mapping will need an explicit definition of “h2”. Studies that report rs2305619 or rs1840680 identify the whole class (A-C-A and A-A-A); studies that report rs3816527 identify only A-C-A. A three-haplotype term would be a sensitivity analysis, not a change to D2.

section: Addendum 3, 18 October 2026: base dataset, twin correction and patient-level bootstrap (D9)

Addendum 3, 18 October 2026: base dataset, twin correction and patient-level bootstrap (D9)
Written after the prespec-lock tag and after addendum 2. No genetic-layer result exists. The MCID rule, the primary threshold, the fixed published equation and every decision above except the baseline cohort and the bootstrap are unchanged.
What prompted it. boscore.xlsx, the parent file of bs.xlsx, became available. It reconciles with bs.xlsx exactly (scripts/08_reconcile_boscore.R checks this and stops if anything changes):

The seven bs.xlsx predictors are the BOSCORE_* columns: BOSCORE_8 uncontrolled malignancy, _9 high-risk chemotherapy, _6 high-dose steroids, _11 severe lymphopenia, _15 CMV, _10 prolonged neutropenia and _4 prior mould disease, with 100% agreement on all 4,127 rows. The outcome matches, and id in bs.xlsx is the row number.
The paper’s analysis set is the 4,127 of the 4,694 rows with complete data on those seven items. All 567 excluded rows have a missing item.
49 admission numbers appear on two rows. In every pair the patient and the predictor profile are identical and exactly one row is an event. So the 4,127 rows are 4,078 unique admissions, and 133 events in 4,078 is 3.26%, the paper’s stated 3.3% (133 in 4,127 is 3.22%). The published equation reproduces only from the rows with the twins in, so it appears to have been fitted with them.


D9. Base dataset and baseline cohort: settled

The base dataset is boscore.xlsx, restricted by the inclusion rule above to the 4,127 rows of the analysis set.
The baseline cohort is the 4,078 unique admissions. For each of the 49 duplicated admission numbers the event row is kept and the non-event twin is dropped. The cohort has 4,078 admissions in 1,945 patients (2.10 per patient) and all 133 events. It replaces the 4,127-row cohort of D8. The 4,127 rows stay as a sensitivity analysis.
The bootstrap resamples patients, with all their admissions, 2,000 resamples. This replaces the admission-level bootstrap of D8, which ignored clustering. The admission-level intervals are kept for comparison.
The MCID rule is unchanged (20% more true cases at no increase in false positives; 5% primary, 20% secondary). Its values are a function of the baseline cohort, so they are re-derived on the new one:

section: Addendum 5, 18 October 2026: the 49 duplicate pairs are confirmed as an artefact
text:
Addendum 5, 18 October 2026: the 49 duplicate pairs are confirmed as an artefact
Written after the tag. The 49 admission numbers that appear on two rows (same patient, identical predictor profile, one event row and one non-event twin) have been confirmed as a recording artefact. This settles the condition left open in D9 and in addendum 3, which said the 4,127-row cohort would become the baseline again if the pairs proved legitimate.

D9 stands. The baseline cohort is the 4,078 unique admissions, and the bootstrap resamples patients. The revert condition no longer applies.
The 4,127-row cohort is now a sensitivity analysis only, which was its role in D9. It is a record of how the paper’s analysis set was built, not an alternative baseline. The D9 commitment to report results against the 4,127-row MCID (+0.00445 at 5%, +0.00142 at 20%) is unchanged. It still brackets the outcome-risk readings of addendum 4, and any decision to drop it should be taken and recorded separately.
Set aside, not pursued: the two Table 2 non-case counts that exceed the file’s by one (high-risk chemotherapy 777 against 776, prolonged neutropenia 1,098 against 1,097), and whether the published equation was fitted with the twin rows in. The analysis uses the counts in the file, and the equation stays fixed at its published coefficients either way, so neither question affects any result. Addenda 3 and 4 mention them as open; this addendum retires them. No request to Bologna remains outstanding.

section: Addendum 7, 18 October 2026: PTX3 h2 defined, and the evidence-to-parameter mapping started (D11)
text:
Addendum 7, 18 October 2026: PTX3 h2 defined, and the evidence-to-parameter mapping started (D11)
Written after the tag. No genetic-layer result exists. Nothing in D1 to D10 changes. This settles the meaning of “h2” that addendum 2 left open, and records the rules for turning extracted evidence into model parameters, with PTX3 as the pilot.

D11. The PTX3 term, and what “h2” means: settled

h2 is the chromosome class that carries the A allele at rs2305619 (forward strand). In the phased 1000G EUR data that is A-C-A (39.8%), A-A-A (5.8%) and A-A-G (0.1%), 45.6% in all; rescaled to gnomAD NFE it is 48.2%. h1 is G-A-G (54.4%, or 51.8% rescaled). The model term is an additive per-copy effect of h2 in the recipient: dosage 0, 1 or 2, on the log-odds scale. The single A-A-G chromosome goes to h2 by the rs2305619 rule.
rs1840680 A marks the same class (r2 = 0.996), so it is an interchangeable tag. The h2 dosage is the number of A alleles at either SNP.
rs3816527 C is not interchangeable. It marks only A-C-A, about 87% of h2. Evidence reported on rs3816527 is mapped to h2 through the haplotype structure, which attenuates a per-copy effect by about 12% at a log OR of 0.8, and is used as a cross-check, not as primary evidence.
A three-haplotype term that separates A-C-A from A-A-A is a sensitivity analysis. It has not been run.

text:
Addendum 8, 18 October 2026: PTX3 rows checked against sources, and the mapping extended to CLEC7A and TLR4 (D12)

Erratum (addendum 16, section 0): the CLEC7A figures below (Y238X OR 0.98, 1.36 with hazard ratios) used Fischer 2016 with its direction reversed; corrected they are 0.84 (0.48 to 1.48) and 1.23 (0.70 to 1.77).

Written after the tag. No genetic-layer result exists. Nothing in D1 to D11 changes, but one statement in addendum 7 is retracted (below). The source checks are read-throughs by the assistant. They are not the human round-2 check, which is still pending, and the two papers were read differently: Herrero-Sanchez 2018 as full text from PMC, Brunel 2018 from a summary of the article page returned by the fetch tool, so its figures and quotes are not verbatim and should be re-read.

Herrero-Sanchez 2018 (S035): corrected, and addendum 7 was wrong about its direction
Addendum 7 said this study “points the other way” (-0.43 per h2 copy) and raised the heterogeneity. That was an artefact. In every table of the paper the reference group is labelled 1.00, but the printed odds ratio belongs to that group against the others. The genotype counts show it: for rs2305619 and the Candida or Aspergillus detection endpoint (Table 3), AA is the “reference”, yet AA has the higher share of cases (23 of 41 against 66 of 157) and the printed 1.83 is the crude 1.76 for AA against the rest, not its reciprocal 0.57. All 18 dominant and recessive odds ratios in Tables 3, 4 and 5 (three SNPs) agree with that reading: 16 decisively, 2 too close to 1 to tell, none contradicting. The paper’s text agrees, calling AA (rs2305619, rs1840680) and CC (rs3816527) the risk genotypes and A-C-A the risk haplotype.
The extraction copied the table faithfully and my parser followed its “(ref)” marker. 30 dominant and recessive rows are now corrected (data/extraction_corrections.csv, each with its evidence and a check that the value it replaces is unchanged). Corrected, the study’s per-copy h2 effect is +0.47 (SE 0.29) on the detection endpoint and +1.16 (SE 0.55) on invasive aspergillosis (Table 5: 12 patients with EORTC/MSG invasive disease), so it agrees in direction with the other studies. Also confirmed: the extracted Table 3 values match the paper, samples were taken before HSCT (a recipient study), and the analysis is adjusted for sex, age and malignancy. The paper prints 1.76 (0.92 to 1.76) for the rs1840680 recessive row, an upper limit equal to the estimate, a printing error in the source. The supplementary CLEC7A tables were not read.
D3b is not changed, but note what it rests on. It excluded this study because its extracted endpoint (Table 3) includes colonisation. Table 5 is an invasive mould endpoint in the whole cohort, and it is in the extraction; it is run as a sensitivity analysis below. Whether the primary analysis should use the Table 5 rows is a question for you.


Brunel 2018 (S029): the design is confirmed, the per-SNP counts cannot be, and one check is worrying
Confirmed from the page: 185 patients and 212 courses (2007 to 2017), 26 probable or proven invasive mould infections (16 probable, 10 proven), all moulds, and an adjusted HR of 5.06 (1.68 to 15.2) without pre-existing neutropenia. The reported minor allele frequencies, 0.48 for rs2305619 and 0.44 for rs3816527, fit A and C as the minor alleles. But the main text gives only a combined exposure (“two copies of the minor allele of rs2305619 and/or rs3816527”); the per-SNP counts are in Online Supplementary Figure S2, an image, so the extracted counts cannot be checked against the text.
A frequency check on the extracted counts raises a doubt. With a minor allele frequency of 0.44 the rs3816527 CC homozygotes should be about 19% of courses, but the extracted “homozygous” group is 30% (z = +4.0 against CC) and fits the major-allele AA homozygotes (31%). It is the same in the two strata (z = +2.7 and +3.1). For rs2305619 the two homozygote shares (23% and 27%) are too close to separate, but the observed 27% fits the major-allele group slightly better. So the extracted groups may not be the minor-allele homozygotes the paper describes, and the sign of Brunel’s effect is not secure. Genotype source is also not stated in the text. This study stays in the primary analysis for now, flagged, and a sensitivity analysis drops it.

The primary analysis is unchanged, because Herrero-Sanchez is outside it (D3b): OR 1.35 per h2 copy (90% interval 0.99 to 1.81), tau 0.17, five studies. 128 of 162 usable rows now map, up from 104, because the cleaned comparison text is readable.

section: Addendum 9, 19 October 2026: CD209, IL10 and IFNG mapped (D13)
text:
Addendum 9, 19 October 2026: CD209, IL10 and IFNG mapped (D13)
Written after the tag. No genetic-layer result exists. Nothing in D1 to D12 changes.
Round-2 status. The user reports that the human checks confirmed the extraction against the source PDFs and that none of the flagged items in addendum 8 changed. No verification record is in the repository, so the extraction used here is still the round-1 file plus the 30 Herrero-Sanchez corrections, and the Brunel, de Boer, rs7309123 strand and Herrero-Sanchez Table 5 questions keep their addendum 8 treatment. The record of the checks should be added to data/ so the claim can be traced.

D13. Decisions made on 19 October 2026

CD209 risk class: chromosomes carrying G at rs4804800 (G-A and G-G, 12.5% in gnomAD NFE). rs4804800 rows map to it directly; rs7248637 rows (A allele, r2 = 0.41) map through the haplotype structure and are used only where a study has no rs4804800 row. A second CD209 parameter is not estimated.
Hazard-ratio rule, per term. Odds-ratio evidence is the primary analysis. If it has fewer than three studies, hazard-ratio studies are added and the scenario is labelled as a fallback. PTX3, CLEC7A and TLR4 are unchanged (all have four or more studies, and their hazard-ratio versions stay sensitivity analyses). The question of Fisher 2017 joining the primary analysis for those terms stays closed.
IL10 and IFNG risk alleles (my choice, open to change): the forward-strand allele most studies report as their effect allele, IL10 C (reported as G) and IFNG G (reported as C). A study that reports the other allele maps to the same class with the sign reversed.



Mapping rule changes
Two changes to the shared code, both checked by re-running scripts 12 and 14, which reproduce every earlier output unchanged (the row-effect files gain one column):

Three more subgroup labels count as whole-cohort analyses: Lupianez 2015’s “patient (recipient) genotype” (phase 1 and overall combined) and Fisher 2017’s “recipient (PT) genotype”. Without them, IFNG lost its only odds-ratio study and Fisher’s CD209 rows were dropped.
Within a study, an “overall combined” analysis is preferred to the phase analyses it contains. Before, the phase 1 additive row outranked the combined dominant row only because of the model-type ordering, which would have used the smaller cohort by accident.

section: Addendum 10, 19 October 2026: IL10 and IFNG dropped from the panel (D14)
text:
Addendum 10, 19 October 2026: IL10 and IFNG dropped from the panel (D14)
Written after the tag. No genetic-layer result exists. This uses the discretion D3 left open (“IL10 rs1800896, IFNG rs2069705: optional, include or drop at the analyst’s discretion”), so no pre-specified decision is reversed.

D14. The panel is the four core terms
IL10 rs1800896 and IFNG rs2069705 are dropped. The genetic layer uses four terms: PTX3 (h2), CLEC7A (Y238X), TLR4 (G-T) and CD209 (G at rs4804800).
Reasons (addendum 9): after the hazard-ratio fallback IL10 rests on one study and IFNG on two, so a pooled value is mostly the prior. IFNG’s two studies disagree in direction. Neither term has enough evidence to estimate an effect or its heterogeneity, and using a prior-dominated draw would add a term whose size is set by the prior rather than the literature.

The mapping outputs (output/il10_*.csv, output/ifng_*.csv) and the code stay in the repository and are described on the evidence-mapping page. They are not read by the genetic layer.
Adding either term back later is a sensitivity analysis, not a change to the primary panel. It needs more studies or an explicit prior for its effect.
Four terms is well inside the roughly ten-parameter ceiling that 133 events supports (D3), which leaves room for the Aim 4 sweep.

section: Addendum 12, 19 October 2026: sampling variability, the correlation ensemble and per-term attribution (D16)
text:
Addendum 12, 19 October 2026: sampling variability, the correlation ensemble and per-term attribution (D16)

Erratum (19 October 2026, addendum 16, section 0): the CLEC7A evidence behind this addendum used one study (Fischer 2016) with its direction reversed. The tables below show the values before the correction; the regenerated files in output/ hold the corrected ones, and the differences are small (gains by at most 0.00006, shares reaching the MCID by at most 3 points, Shapley shares by at most 1.6 points). The conclusions do not change.

Written after the tag. Provisional, like addendum 11: the effects come from the provisional evidence mapping, and the design below is my proposal. Nothing in D1 to D15 changes. The addendum 11 results reproduce unchanged after the code was extended.

D16. Design (proposed)

Correlation ensemble (sensitivity analysis, D8 and D9). Each simulated world draws one of the 150 near-optimal copula matrices (script 02) and uses its exact profile distribution (cached in output/correlation_ensemble_profile_probs.csv; total-variation distance to the empirical distribution 0.08 to 0.19, median 0.12). The refit baseline and the published marginals are unchanged. The MCID is the one of the baseline in that member’s own distribution (+0.00488 at 5% and +0.00188 at 20% at the ensemble median, against +0.00458 and +0.00160 on the empirical cohort). 3,000 worlds per reading, 20 per member.
Attribution. Shapley decomposition of the gain into the four terms. The value of a subset of terms is the gain of a score that carries only those effects (recentred), under the full true model. The four contributions sum to the gain of the full score. Net benefit is a threshold rule on a sum of effects, so it is not additive in the terms, and the Shapley split is a fair division of the total, not a separable effect. Run on the empirical cohort for 1,000 draws per reading, for the ceiling and the realised score.
Sampling variability. Each simulated study resamples patients with their admissions (so the clinical mix varies: about 4,078 admissions, 1,945 patients, 133 events), gives each patient a genotype, draws outcomes from the true risk, and measures the observed gain in net benefit of a fixed score over the baseline in that sample. Scores are not refitted in the sample. Four runs of 2,000 studies: effects fixed at the pooled medians, effects fixed at the 95th percentile of each term’s pooled effect (a favourable truth), and effects drawn from the posteriors under the two readings. The ensemble and the sampling variability are not combined: the studies resample the real cohort.
Sensitivity cohorts (added later on 19 October). The same three analyses on three further settings, with the same effects, seeds and pooled estimates, so the settings differ only in the cohort and the baseline model: the published equation on the 4,078-admission base cohort, the published equation on the 4,127 rows of the paper (twin rows kept; the D8 baseline), and a refit on the 4,127 rows. The last is my addition, to separate the effect of the cohort from the effect of the equation. Each setting uses its own MCID, which reproduces the values in D8 and D9: +0.00404 and +0.00113 (published, 4,078), +0.00445 and +0.00142 (published, 4,127), +0.00440 and +0.00141 (refit, 4,127), against +0.00458 and +0.00160 for the primary setting (refit, 4,078). text:
Addendum 13, 19 October 2026: the ensemble with the sampling variability, and donor genotype in the allo-HSCT stratum (D17)

Erratum (19 October 2026, addendum 16, section 0): the CLEC7A evidence behind this addendum used one study (Fischer 2016) with its direction reversed. The tables below show the values before the correction; the regenerated files in output/ hold the corrected ones, and the differences are small (gains by at most 0.00006, shares reaching the MCID by at most 3 points, Shapley shares by at most 1.6 points). The conclusions do not change.

Written after the tag. Provisional, like addenda 11 and 12. Nothing in D1 to D16 changes, and the primary results of addenda 11 and 12 reproduce unchanged.

D17. Design (proposed)
Ensemble with sampling variability. Each simulated study draws one of the 150 copula members and builds its clinical mix from it. The patients are resampled from the real admissions-per-patient counts (so the genotype clustering is kept), and each admission’s profile is drawn independently from the member’s distribution. This ignores any covariate correlation within a patient. The truth, the recentring and the MCID are the member’s own (+0.00488 at 5%, +0.00188 at 20%). Two controls: the same simulation with the empirical profile distribution in place of a member, and the real-row resampling of addendum 12. 2,000 studies per run.
Donor genotype in the allo-HSCT stratum (D1, secondary analysis).

The stratum. The base cohort has no admission-level allo-HSCT flag (the column names of boscore.xlsx hold only a transplant date, DTMO, and the pseudonymised full BOSCORE file that has allogeneic_hsct cannot be linked to it). I did not read any value from the identified file. The stratum is built from the published Table 1 margins (allo is the reason for admission in 44 of 133 cases and 248 of 3,994 non-cases) under the assumption that allo status depends on the outcome only, given the clinical profile. That gives a stratum of 7.1% of admissions (289 of 4,078, 44 expected events), an event rate of 15.2% (Table 1: 15.1%), a profile mix tilted to higher-risk profiles, and a true risk whose odds are the baseline score’s times 5.3 at every profile.
The scores. The Stanzani score has no allo item, so the baseline decides as before and under-predicts in the stratum. In the stratum it flags 22% of admissions at 5%, and finds 107 true cases and 118 false positives per 1,000 allo admissions. The genetic scores add donor genotype, with the donor effects, to the baseline logit and are recentred to the baseline score’s mean risk (D5), so they carry no information about allo status itself.
The truth. Baseline logit plus the allo offset plus donor effects, recentred to hold the stratum’s event rate. Donor dosage is Hardy-Weinberg with the same class frequencies (unrelated donors, independent of the recipient’s profile). The recipient effects are not used in the stratum.
The gain is per allo admission. The whole-cohort equivalent is the gain times 7.1%, with decisions elsewhere left to the baseline. The stratum MCID is 20% more true cases among its admissions at no extra false positives, from its own baseline: +0.02137 at 5% (21 extra cases per 1,000 allo admissions) and +0.00747 at 20%. The whole-cohort MCID of D10 is also shown.

At the 5% threshold, donor genotype adds about 3 to 4 true cases per 1,000 allo admissions in the median world, against the 21 needed. The gain does not reach the stratum MCID in any scenario (0% to 0.4% of worlds, and at most 9% of simulated studies even when every effect is at its 95th percentile).
At 20% the stratum MCID is smaller (+0.00747, about 7.5 extra cases per 1,000) and the ceiling score reaches it in 55% to 66% of worlds. A score that uses the pooled estimates reaches it in 3% to 7%. The gain per allo admission is larger than the recipient gain per admission (+0.0033 against +0.0006 at 5%) because the stratum has a much higher event rate (15%).
Spread over the whole cohort the donor gain is small: +0.0002 to +0.0003 at 5% and +0.0004 to +0.0007 at 20%, at most 4% of worlds reach the whole-cohort MCID.
A study of 289 admissions and 44 events is very noisy. The SD of the observed gain at 5% (0.0038 at the pooled medians) exceeds the expected gain (+0.0025), and only 57% of studies show a positive gain.



Limits and what would change them

The allo flag (superseded by addendum 14, which builds the stratum from the data and finds this assumption does not hold). The stratum’s profile mix and its constant odds multiplier of 5.3 rest on one assumption: that allo status is independent of the clinical profile once the outcome is known. If allo recipients’ excess risk comes mostly through the predictors (more steroids, neutropenia, CMV), the true multiplier would be smaller and the stratum would sit at higher-risk profiles, which changes both the baseline’s performance and the MCID. An admission-level allo flag in the analysis file would replace this assumption. I do not know whether boscore.xlsx carries one (its column names show only DTMO, a transplant date, which would not separate allogeneic from autologous), and I did not read values from it. If you add the flag to the pseudonymised base cohort (script 08) the stratum can be built from the data.
The donor evidence is one study each for PTX3 and CLEC7A, two for TLR4, none for CD209, and one of them is a hazard ratio. The pooled donor intervals are wide, and the CLEC7A value (OR 0.70) rests on one study with a wide interval.
Donors are taken as unrelated (independent of the recipient’s genotype) and each admission as having its own donor. A matched sibling donor shares half of the recipient’s alleles.
Donor and recipient effects are not combined: in the stratum the score uses donor effects only. The Shapley attribution is not repeated for the donor analysis.

text:
Addendum 14, 19 October 2026: an admission-level allo-HSCT flag, and the donor-genotype stratum rebuilt from the data (D18)

Erratum (19 October 2026, addendum 16, section 0): the CLEC7A evidence behind this addendum used one study (Fischer 2016) with its direction reversed. The tables below show the values before the correction; the regenerated files in output/ hold the corrected ones, and the differences are small (gains by at most 0.00006, shares reaching the MCID by at most 3 points, Shapley shares by at most 1.6 points). The conclusions do not change.

Written after the tag. Provisional, like addenda 11 to 13. Nothing in D1 to D17 changes, and the addendum 11 and 12 results reproduce unchanged. It supersedes the stratum construction of addendum 13, which is kept as a sensitivity analysis.

The flag
boscore.xlsx has no allo-HSCT column. What it has, and what was used (script 08, the identified file read locally; only counts were printed and no date or identifier is kept):

SCORE9 (recode2SCORE9, coded 2) is the older item “allo-HSCT, or high-dose cytarabine, FLAI-E or ICE chemotherapy”. The item named allogeneic_hsct in the 2019 file is the same column (862 of the 863 admissions coded 2 are flagged in the 2019 file, and none of the 3,264 coded 0 is). The 2017 high-risk chemotherapy item (BOSCORE_9) is this item: they differ on 2 of 4,127 rows.
DTMO is a transplant date, present on 1,124 of the 4,127 rows and always 0 to 365 days after the admission date (mostly 1 to 30). Autologous transplants sit in the other category of SCORE9, so a transplant date on a row of the composite category marks an allo-HSCT admission.
The flag is therefore SCORE9 = 2 and a transplant date present (allo_hsct_flag() in R/boscore_data.R). Only whether the date is present is used.

Validation against Table 1 (allo-HSCT as the reason for admission: 292 admissions, 44 events, 248 non-events): the flag gives 292 admissions, exactly, with 43 events and 249 non-events, one admission classed the other way. That is the same size of discrepancy as the two Table 2 counts that are one lower than published (D8), and is recorded as a known difference (BOSCORE_EXPECTED). The flag is added to the pseudonymised base cohort (data/restricted/base_cohort_pseudonymised.csv, column allo_hsct; a file without it still loads, with the flag missing) and the counts are in output/allo_hsct_summary.csv.
In the base cohort of 4,078 unique admissions there are 272 allo-HSCT admissions with 43 events (6.7% of admissions, event rate 15.8%). 20 of the 49 non-event twin rows are allo admissions (41%, against 7% overall), so the duplicate-pair artefact (addendum 5) is concentrated in transplant admissions.

section: Addendum 15, 19 October 2026: Aim 3b started, the expected direction stated before the run (D19)
text:
Addendum 15, 19 October 2026: Aim 3b started, the expected direction stated before the run (D19)
Written after the tag and before any Aim 3b result exists. This section (prediction and design) was committed and pushed first, so the prediction cannot be adjusted to the results. Results follow in a later section of this addendum. Provisional, like addenda 11 to 14.

What Aim 3b is, and the tension
Aim 3b is a neutropenia-stratified falsification test (project description). Feys and colleagues found that PTX3 and CLEC7A variants do not predispose to influenza- or COVID-associated aspergillosis, and explain it by inflammatory levelling: severe viral pneumonia induces PTX3 as an acute-phase protein, so genotype-determined baseline differences are swamped. Neutropenia is used as a proxy for the non-inflamed host, not as a claim that the effects are neutrophil-dependent. The hypothesis under test, H_F, is therefore that per-copy genetic effects are larger in neutropenic than in non-neutropenic admissions. The only direct stratified evidence, Brunel 2018 (supplementary figure, transcribed by an agent, derived by subtraction and flagged ambiguous), points the other way: the PTX3 homozygote contrast is significant in the non-neutropenic stratum (P = 0.008 and 0.002 for the two SNPs) and not in the neutropenic one (P = 0.7 and 0.6). Its stratum is neutropenia at presentation (ANC below 500), which is not the cohort’s prolonged-neutropenia predictor, so even that evidence is not like for like.


What the simulation can and cannot do
The effect modification is an input of the simulation, so the simulation cannot decide between Feys and Brunel. It can show (i) what each reading would mean for decisions, at the same pooled effect; (ii) what it costs to build a stratified score on the wrong reading; and (iii) whether a study of this size could tell the readings apart, which is the question that matters for a falsification test.


Expected direction (written before the run)








#
prediction
confidence




E1
The effect-modification ratio estimated from Brunel’s counts (neutropenic over non-neutropenic) has a point estimate below 1, the opposite of H_F, with an interval that includes 1
high for the sign of the point estimate, high that the interval includes 1


E2
With homogeneous effects, the gain per admission is larger in the neutropenic stratum, because it holds most of the events, and the neutropenic stratum contributes more than its share of admissions (about a quarter) to the whole-cohort gain
medium


E3
At the same pooled effect, a truth in the H_F direction gives a larger whole-cohort gain than a truth in the Brunel direction at the 20% threshold, because the effects sit where the events are. At 5% the baseline probably already flags most neutropenic admissions (as in the allo stratum), leaving little room, so I do not commit to a direction at 5%
low to medium at 20%, none at 5%


E4
A stratified score built on the wrong reading loses gain: under a Brunel-direction truth, a score that assumes H_F does worse than the common-effect score, and the reverse
high, qualitatively


E5
The falsification test is underpowered in a study of this size (133 events). Fitting a genotype-by-neutropenia interaction in simulated studies, the estimate has the true sign in at most about 75% of studies under a moderate modification (ratio 4 or 1/4), and the interaction reaches P < 0.05 in at most 15%
medium



So the expected headline is: the neutropenia split matters less than the question of whether the whole-cohort pooled effects are right, and a study of this size could not confirm or reject H_F. If E1 holds, the available evidence leans against H_F, but weakly.


D19. Design (proposed; fixed before the run)

Strata. The prolonged-neutropenia predictor of the base cohort (4,078 admissions): neutropenic and non-neutropenic. The decision rule is the refit baseline in both. Each stratum has its own profile distribution, share, and event rate.
Truth. Stratum-specific per-copy effects, beta_N and beta_NN, with the event-weighted average equal to the pooled effect beta, so the whole-cohort pooled evidence stays consistent: w beta_N + (1 - w) beta_NN = beta, where w is the share of the baseline’s events that fall in the neutropenic stratum. The modification ratio r = beta_N / beta_NN takes the values infinity (all in neutropenic admissions), 4, 1 (homogeneous, as in addenda 11 to 14), 1/4 and 0 (all in non-neutropenic), plus a data-based value: r drawn from the Brunel counts, log r ~ N(estimate, SE). The truth is recentred within each stratum to hold that stratum’s event rate (D5). Effects are drawn from the pooled posteriors as before (mean reading, 1,000 draws).
Scores (fixed, not fitted): the baseline; the ceiling (true stratum-specific effects, an oracle that knows the modification); the common score (pooled medians in both strata, the “realised” score of the earlier addenda); and assumed-H_F and assumed-Brunel scores (pooled medians distributed between the strata as ratios of 4 and 1/4 would imply). Each is recentred to its stratum’s baseline mean risk.
Outcomes. Net-benefit gain over the baseline in each stratum (per stratum admission) and for the whole cohort (shares times the stratum gains, a single threshold), at 5% (primary) and 20% (secondary), against the whole-cohort MCID (+0.00458, +0.00160) and each stratum’s own MCID (20% more true cases among its admissions at no extra false positives).
The falsification test. In each simulated study of 4,078 admissions (patients resampled, genotype per patient, outcomes from the truth), a logistic model with the baseline logit as an offset, outcome ~ offset(logit) + S + S:N, where S is the pooled-median genetic score and N the neutropenia indicator. The interaction coefficient is the estimated modification on the log-odds scale. Reported: the share of studies in which it has the true sign, and the share with P < 0.05 in the true direction. 1,000 studies per truth.
Not included: per-term attribution, the correlation ensemble, the sensitivity cohorts, donor genotype, and any link between genotype and neutropenia (genotype is independent of the clinical profile, as before).



Results (written after the run)
Changes to the plan, and one error found.

The data-based Brunel scenario was planned as a ratio drawn with log r ~ N(estimate, SE). The estimate is negative (ratio -0.11), so its logarithm does not exist, and holding the pooled effect as the event-weighted average would need an effect 8.6 times the pooled one in the non-neutropenic stratum (the Bologna event share in neutropenic admissions is 0.80, Brunel’s about 0.4). The scenario instead applies Brunel’s stratum effects directly, as fractions of its own whole-cohort effect: -0.21 in neutropenic admissions and +1.87 in non-neutropenic ones, which leaves a whole-cohort effect of about 0.2 of the pooled one.
The first run of the interaction fit left the neutropenia main effect out of the model. The truth is recentred within each stratum, so the strata differ in intercept, and the omission pulled the interaction estimate towards zero (it recovered about a third of the true difference). A check against known truths on a large replicated cohort found it. All interaction results below are from the corrected model, and the layer results were not affected.
The recentring bracket was widened (an effect several times the pooled one in the small non-neutropenic stratum needs a shift beyond 8 on the logit scale). The earlier results are unchanged.

The strata. Neutropenic admissions are 28% of the cohort (1,157), with a baseline event rate of 9.2% and 106 of the 133 events (80%). Non-neutropenic admissions are 72% (2,921), with an event rate of 0.9% and 27 events. The stratum MCIDs are +0.01516 (5%) and +0.00553 (20%) for neutropenic admissions, and +0.00039 and +0.00004 for non-neutropenic ones, where there are so few events that almost any gain clears them.
E1, the Brunel evidence. Mapped to the per-copy h2 scale, Brunel’s PTX3 effect is +1.17 (SE 0.49) in the non-neutropenic stratum and -0.13 (SE 0.53) in the neutropenic stratum (rs2305619), a difference of -1.30 (SE 0.72; 95% interval -2.71 to +0.12; P = 0.07). Through rs3816527 it is +1.76 (SE 0.86) and -0.24 (SE 0.54), a difference of -1.99 (SE 1.01; 95% interval -3.98 to -0.01; P = 0.049). The point estimates are opposite to H_F, as predicted. The interval includes no difference for rs2305619 but only just excludes it for rs3816527, so “the interval includes 1” holds for one of the two SNPs. The data are 212 courses and 26 events, the stratum is neutropenia at presentation (not the cohort’s prolonged-neutropenia item), and the counts have the doubts recorded in addendum 8.
Net-benefit gain, whole cohort (mean reading, 1,000 draws, median; the 90% ranges, the predictive reading and the stratum results are in output/aim3b_layer_summary.csv). The ceiling score knows the true stratum effects, the common score applies the pooled estimates to everyone, and the assumed scores split the pooled estimates between the strata as a ratio of 4 (assumed H_F) or 1/4 (assumed Brunel) would imply:

At the 95th-percentile effects the power rises (97% for all-in-neutropenic, 82% for ratio 4). The interaction fit is unbiased and its false-positive rate is about 5%, as it should be.
